newsitem.title: USA: U.S. urges Russia to scrap India nuclear deal.
newsitem.headline: U.S. urges Russia to scrap India nuclear deal.

text.p: The United States has urged Russia to drop its planned sale of two light-water nuclear reactors to India, saying it violates an international agreement, the New York Times reported on Thursday.
The newspaper quoted an unidentified senior U.S. official as saying the sale would be a setback for worldwide efforts to stop the spread of nuclear weapons.

"There are two basic problems," the official said. "One is the Indians. We worry about what the Indians will do with the reactors. We worry about the safety culture. Even a light-water reactor produces a fair amount of plutonium."
The official said the other problem was that the "Russian Federation, as signatories to the 1992 suppliers' agreement, should not be selling these controlled nuclear technologies."

The suppliers agreement forbids suppliers from exporting nuclear technology to aspiring nuclear powers. Sales are forbidden to countries not formally recognized as nuclear weapons states and which do not allow international inspections of key nuclear institutes.
Only the United States, Russia, Britain, France and China are recognized as nuclear weapons states.

Russian officials insisted the sale to India should be exempted from the agreement because it was included in an earlier understanding between then-President Mikhail Gorbachev and Indian leaders, the newspaper said. The initial agreement to build the reactors was worked out in 1987.

The New York Times reported that Yevgeny Reshetnikov, a deputy minister of Russia's Atomic Energy Agency, said in an interview that the value of the sale to India was $1.5 billion to $2 billion for each of the light-water reactors.

The reactors, to be installed in southern India, can produce one million kilowatts each. Light-water reactors use ordinary water to slow down the neutrons emitted by nuclear fission to the speed required to sustain the chain reaction.
The paper reported that Indian officials said they needed nuclear plants because of their shortage of electric power and say Washington's arms control policies reflect a colonialist double standard.
